name: validation over a lifetime, for any entity (P19 0.2.0)

R4.why: Own time, own kit, the stack's own governance.

R9.why: Evidence about the stack's own code only.

answers: Ask, before and across the life of anything James builds (a stack layer, a project, a product, a business idea), whether it should be built, whether it is still used, still conforms and still has a reason to be here.

answers.start: Keep asking whether each layer still earns its place.
whys: Because layers stay after their reason has gone, and chains grow until a consolidation.
Because 0.1.0 judges a layer once, at birth, and never again.
Because nothing in the stack turns its own evidence (imports, tests, attacks) into a judgement about why a layer is here.
Because the stack's trust maths (Weight, Trust, Leighton) has only been pointed at claims about the world, never at claims the stack makes about itself.
Because the stack has never been asked to justify itself; James's memory has done that job.

answers:
No automatic removal of anything.
No call counting.
No new maths: Leighton V2 as it is.
No signing on the VPS.
James gets a short list each day of the claims, about layers or about the projects he is building, that are unknown or doubted, with the evidence; and the Field shows which projects still hold.
By 2027-03-31, at least 2 layers or projects are kept, consolidated, parked or retired because the Relevance section asked, and no question in 90 days was raised by a broken measurement.
James decides. The VPS report and the Field show it. Nobody outside James is waiting for it.
James owns it and signs every keep, consolidate or retire.
Runs inside the daily Saboteur report on the VPS; answers are given on the laptop. A broken run shows as a RED report.
If it is wrong, it asks about a layer that is fine (James answers once) or misses one that has gone stale; nothing is removed without James.
James's time answering questions, a few a week at most. The computation is local and adds seconds to the daily report.
Saves the day of rework a late consolidation costs; doing nothing means stale layers pile up until a chain forces a consolidation, as with the Saboteur.
James's memory, a quarterly manual review, a dependency analyser that finds unused imports, or doing nothing. Could reuse an open-source dependency analyser for the import graph.
Leighton V2 unchanged. λ never stored. No key on the VPS. Spare time only.

Evidence about the stack's own code is public-safe. Runs and claims about James's other entities (projects, business ideas, career decisions) stay private in ~/.forge/validation/ and never leave the laptop.
P10, P11, P14 (the stack's own); the VPS check and the Saboteur rotation for evidence; Python's ast module for the import graph. All replaceable and local.
About 30 repositories and a handful of projects, a few claims each: a few hundred claims; at 10x it is still seconds.

1. Claims with λ through Leighton V2, asked in the daily report and the Field
2. A quarterly manual review using the checklist's retro
3. Reuse an open-source dependency analyser for unused code only
4. Don't build it, park it: keep 0.1.0's birth-only validation

Option 1 uses the stack's own maths but needs evidence weights that are guesses at first. A manual review needs memory and discipline. A dependency analyser answers 'is it imported', not 'why is it here'. Parking leaves life and death to memory.

answers.chosen: Claims with λ through Leighton V2, asked in the daily report and the Field
answers.rejected: Quarterly manual review; dependency analyser only; park it
answers.reason: It uses the stack's own trust maths on the stack's own evidence, and a quiet layer drifts to unknown, not to distrusted.
answers.downside: The evidence weights and half-lives are guesses until 90 days of outcomes calibrate them.
answers.trigger: If more than 3 questions in the first 30 days come from a broken measurement, stop and recalibrate before going on.

answers: The import graph and 'reached on a real path', claims from runs and SPECs, λ through Leighton V2, and the Relevance section in the daily report, by 2027-01-31.

The import graph from the real entry points can be built statically.
Leighton V2's domain registry gives per-kind decay without changes.
The evidence weights give sensible λ on the existing layers.

Build the import graph statically from the entry points and compare it with a hand check of 5 layers; compute λ through Leighton V2's domain registry on the existing layers in a dry run; James reviews the evidence weights and the dry-run list before anything is shown daily.
The Relevance section lists each question with its λ and evidence; a dry run that asks about a layer James knows is in use shows the weights or the import graph are broken.
The import graph or the evidence weights are wrong, so the stack asks about layers that are in use and James stops reading the section.

answers.start: The stack asks about layers that are in use.
whys: Because the import graph misses a real path, such as a dynamic import or a sibling found through sys.path.
Because the layers find each other through sys.path inserts and FORGE_LEGACY_ROOT, which a static graph cannot always see.

answers: A layer could be made to look used with a dummy import from an entry point; the import graph records the path, so the reason is visible.
When a question comes from a missed real path, add the sys.path and FORGE_LEGACY_ROOT resolution to the import graph, record the missed path as a test, and recompute.
James approves the evidence weights, the half-lives and every signed answer; the weights live in one file in the layer; the CHANGELOG records each change.
The claims, the evidence table and the report explain themselves; no handover capsule yet.
One command prints the Relevance section for the whole stack.

answers.signal: By 2027-03-31 no layer has been kept, consolidated or retired because of a question, or James has stopped answering for 30 days
answers.then: James decides: keep, recalibrate, or retire 0.2.0 back to birth-only validation.
